questions.q: What if I was partially at fault for the accident?
questions.a: Texas’s comparative fault rule allows recovery even if you share some responsibility, as long as your portion of fault is below 51 percent. However, the compensation you receive will be reduced by your percentage of fault. This makes accurate liability analysis critical.

questions.q: What if I wasn’t wearing a helmet when the crash happened?
questions.a: Not wearing a helmet does not automatically prevent you from recovering compensation. It may become an issue the insurance company raises to argue that your injuries were worse than they would have been with a helmet, which can affect the value of the claim depending on the facts.

questions.q: What if the insurance company says I was partly at fault?
questions.a: Under Texas’s comparative fault rules, you can still recover compensation as long as you are found 50% or less responsible for the crash, though your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. Disputed liability does not automatically mean you have no case, particularly when the insurance company’s version of events isn’t supported by the evidence.

covers.title: Helmet requirements under Texas law

covers.title: Lane splitting and lane filtering

covers.title: Comparative fault and the 51% rule
covers.text: Compensation is reduced by your share of fault, and a rider found more than 50% responsible cannot recover.

covers.title: The two-year deadline to file

questions.q: Can I still have a case if the property owner says the hazard was obvious?
questions.a: Possibly. The owner’s characterization does not determine the issue by itself. Texas generally does not impose a duty to warn an invitee about a condition that was actually open and obvious or already known to the person, but whether a condition meets that standard can depend on the specific circumstances.

questions.q: What if I’m not sure the property owner even knew about the hazard?
questions.a: Constructive knowledge, meaning the hazard existed long enough that a reasonable inspection should have caught it, can satisfy this requirement even without proof the owner had actually noticed it beforehand. This is often the central issue in a premises liability investigation.

questions.q: What if the store says the hazard was obvious?
questions.a: An obvious hazard does not automatically eliminate a claim. Texas law still considers whether the property owner should have fixed or better warned about the condition, and whether the injured person’s own actions contributed to what happened.

questions.q: What if I fell at a store that says they were not notified about the hazard?
questions.a: A property owner does not need direct notice from an employee to be responsible. If a hazard existed long enough that reasonable inspection should have caught it, that may support a claim even without a specific complaint on file.

questions.q: What if my fall happened at a shopping center with multiple businesses?
questions.a: When a fall happens in a shared area, such as a parking lot or common walkway, more than one party may share responsibility, including individual tenants and the property management company. Identifying every responsible party can affect what compensation may be available.

questions.q: Can I still have a case if there were no witnesses?
questions.a: A lack of witnesses does not automatically prevent a claim. Photos taken after the fall, medical records, and the injured person’s own account can all help establish what happened, depending on the facts.

questions.q: What if you were partly at fault for the attack?
questions.a: Common arguments insurance adjusters make involve accusing the victim of either provoking the dog, ignoring warning signs, or trespassing. However, even if you share responsibility, under Texas’s comparative negligence rules , you can still recover compensation if you’re less than 50 percent at fault. Comparative fault applies differently depending on whether your claim relies on Texas’s one-bite rule or is a regular negligence claim.

questions.q: Will my dog bite case go to court?
questions.a: Most dog bite claims resolve through negotiation with the insurance company. We prepare every case as though it may need to go to court, which puts us in a stronger position if the insurer will not offer a fair settlement.

questions.q: What if my child needs future reconstructive surgery?
questions.a: Additional procedures are sometimes required years after a child is bitten due to facial and hand scarring changing as they grow. We document injuries thoroughly and factor in future care when we evaluate the value of your dog bite claim.

about.title: About Joe I. Zaid & Associates
text: Joe I. Zaid & Associates was founded on a simple idea. Injured people deserve the kind of representation you would want for your own family, not standard insurance claim handling.

Since founding the firm in 2013, Joe I. Zaid & Associates has recovered millions of dollars in settlements for injured clients, including numerous seven figure results for individual clients. Before he represented his first injured client, Joe spent nearly a decade inside one of the world’s largest insurance companies, and he built the firm around what that taught him about how insurers evaluate, delay, and dispute claims.

From the first day of a case, the firm works to confirm liability, preserve evidence before it disappears, and identify every insurance policy that may apply. The firm takes every case seriously, whether it settles at the negotiating table or requires litigation.

faqs.q: How do I know if I have a personal injury case?
faqs.a: If another party’s negligence caused your injury and you have losses like medical bills, missed work, or ongoing pain, you likely have grounds worth reviewing. The clearest way to understand whether you may have a case is to have an attorney look at the specific facts, since disputed liability or limited documentation doesn’t automatically rule out a claim.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to hire a personal injury lawyer?
faqs.a: Joe I. Zaid & Associates handles personal injury cases on a contingency fee basis, so you pay no upfront attorney’s fees, and we only get paid if we recover compensation for you.

faqs.q: How much is my personal injury case worth?
faqs.a: There’s no fixed number. Value depends on medical treatment and future care, lost income, the severity of the injury, and available insurance coverage, among other factors. An attorney can give you a realistic picture only after reviewing the details.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Texas?
faqs.a: In most cases, Texas law gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a personal injury lawsuit, under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.003. Certain situations, like claims involving a minor, can affect how that deadline applies.

faqs.q: What should I do after an accident in Houston?
faqs.a: The priorities right after an accident are safety and medical attention, even if injuries don’t seem serious at first. Once you’re safe, documenting the scene, getting a police report, and avoiding early recorded statements to an insurance adjuster can all help protect a future claim.

faqs.q: Will my personal injury case go to trial?
faqs.a: Most personal injury cases settle before trial, but that depends on whether an insurer is willing to offer a fair resolution. Preparing every case with the readiness to litigate, not just negotiate, tends to support a stronger settlement position.

faqs.q: How long does a personal injury case take?
faqs.a: Timelines vary with the complexity of the case, the severity of the injury, how long treatment takes, and whether the insurance company disputes liability. Some cases resolve in a few months, while more serious or contested claims take longer.
